summary: Explains how a SIP user agent obtains and uses a Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU), an address that anyone can use to reach that one specific device instance rather than just the person.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP address of record may reach several devices, while some requests need to reach one device only. A GRUU is a globally usable SIP URI that routes to one user-agent instance.

subtitle: A globally usable SIP address that identifies one specific user-agent instance.

tldr.problem: A SIP address of record can reach several devices for one user, but applications such as call transfer may need to reach one specific device instance from anywhere.
tldr.mechanism: A user agent registers an instance ID and receives public and temporary Globally Routable User Agent URIs. Both identify a specific instance, and a proxy maps them to that instance's registered contact.
tldr.outcome: A user agent can share an address that lets another SIP user agent reach the intended device. RFC 5627 is a Proposed Standard and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

facts.label: Valid GRUU with no contacts response

today: RFC 5627 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Device Needs Its Own SIP Address
sections.content:
A SIP Address of Record (AOR) can represent a user with several user agents, such as handsets, softphones or voicemail accounts. Some operations need a URI that reaches one particular user-agent instance rather than any device associated with the AOR.

RFC 5627 calls this URI a Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU). It is designed to be usable by any user agent on the Internet. Unlike a contact that exposes an IP address or hostname, a GRUU routes through a proxy in the domain that issued it, which maps it to the registered contact for the correct instance.
sections.plainLanguage: A user's AOR can point to several devices, but a call transfer may need one particular device. A GRUU gives that device an address that other SIP users can use.

sections.title: Public and Temporary GRUUs
sections.content:
Every GRUU is a SIP URI containing the gr URI parameter, with or without a value. A public GRUU adds a gr value to the AOR, so removing the parameter yields the AOR. The registrar chooses that value to represent the user-agent instance.

A temporary GRUU hides the AOR from a recipient. It may have other content, as long as it routes to the same specific instance and does not readily reveal the AOR. A registrar often constructs temporary GRUUs using protected stateless values to avoid keeping excessive state.
sections.plainLanguage: A public GRUU includes the AOR, while a temporary GRUU hides it. Both contain the gr parameter and route to one user-agent instance.

sections.title: Requesting GRUUs During Registration
sections.content:
To request GRUUs, a user agent includes the gruu option tag in Supported and provides an instance ID in the +sip.instance Contact parameter. The registrar may return pub-gruu and temp-gruu Contact parameters with the public and temporary URIs.

A user agent must treat the user and host parts of a returned GRUU as opaque and must not modify them. A successful refresh returns the same public GRUU in the usual case and a new temporary GRUU. Temporary GRUUs remain valid while a contact for that instance stays registered and the Call-ID is not changed. Changing the Call-ID invalidates earlier temporary GRUUs.
sections.plainLanguage: The user agent identifies itself when it registers and asks whether the registrar supports GRUUs. The registrar can return two addresses: one that shows the AOR and one that hides it.

sections.title: Using a GRUU in SIP Requests
sections.content:
A user agent should use one of its GRUUs in Contact headers of dialog-forming and target-refresh requests and responses. It must have an active registration before using a GRUU obtained from that registration, and must not reuse a GRUU from a registration that has lapsed. For anonymous requests, the RFC recommends a temporary GRUU.

A request sent to a URI containing gr is expected to reach a specific instance. A user agent should not apply non-standard URI handling to such a URI. When displaying a GRUU to a person, the RFC recommends removing the gr parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: A user agent can put its GRUU in a Contact header so another participant can reach that instance later. It should use a temporary GRUU when it needs to hide the AOR.

sections.title: Registrar Responsibilities and Validity
sections.content:
A registrar associates each GRUU with one AOR and one instance ID. The AOR can resolve to all registered contacts, but the GRUU resolves only to contacts with its instance ID. A registrar ignores any pub-gruu or temp-gruu value supplied by the user agent; the registrar creates the GRUUs itself.

Temporary GRUUs are invalidated when no contact for the instance remains registered, or when the registration Call-ID changes. A public GRUU should remain valid while its AOR is valid, even if it currently has no contacts; requests in that period should receive 480 Temporarily Unavailable. A registrar-issued GRUU's domain must resolve on the public Internet and requests must reach an authoritative proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrar ties each GRUU to one AOR and one device instance. Temporary GRUUs expire with the registration, while a public GRUU can remain valid when the device is temporarily unregistered.

sections.title: How a Proxy Delivers a Request
sections.content:
An authoritative proxy checks whether a Request-URI containing gr matches a valid GRUU in its domain. An unknown or invalid GRUU should receive 404 Not Found. For a valid GRUU, the proxy looks up the URI and rewrites the Request-URI to the matching registered contact.

If no contact is bound to the GRUU, the proxy must return 480 Temporarily Unavailable. With multiple contacts, it follows RFC 5626's reg-id rules when present; otherwise it selects the most recently refreshed contact. It should try another contact after 408 or 430, but not after other responses. Call forwarding should not be applied because the GRUU targets one specific instance.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy checks the GRUU, finds the registered contact for its device instance and sends the request there. It does not forward the request to a different device when the target is unavailable.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of GRUUs
sections.content:
A modified GRUU in a registration response could prevent the user agent from being reached. The RFC recommends using the SIPS URI scheme when registering. Requests to a GRUU should also receive screening so that a guessable public GRUU does not bypass a user's blocking settings.

Temporary GRUUs hide the AOR and instance ID from the Contact value, but reusing one lets correspondents link calls to the same device. Using a different temporary GRUU for each call prevents that correlation from the Contact alone. Other information, such as IP addresses in SDP, can still reveal information about the user agent.
sections.plainLanguage: A temporary GRUU can hide the user's AOR, but reusing it lets recipients recognize the same device across calls. Network details in other SIP data may still reveal information.
